catalog_quote: 4.2. Stress assignment: In Azerbaijani words, stress usually falls on the last syllable except when it is stopped before a number of suffixes which after Lightner (1972), we call 'unstressable suffixes.' E.g., a word like alɨšdɨlar 'they were kindled' is stressed on the vowel of the last syllable because, with regard to stress assignment in Azerbaijani, word boundary plays the role of the sole unstressable unit in this word. But in alɨšmadɨlar 'they were not kindled' the main stress has been stopped by -ma (negative marker) which is one of the unstressable suffixes. [p.116] ... Main stress assignment in Azerbaijani seems to be adequately describable by Lightner's (1972:357) Turkish stress rule: (MSR) V → [+stress] / —C0 [-MSR], where [-MSR] stands for any unit which is an exception to MSR, and the application of the rule is iterative, right-to-left. [p.117] ... 4.2.1. The MSR of Azerbaijani seems to be almost exceptionless. The few exceptions to it, too, appear to be classifiable into two groups: (1) those words that are always stressed on the initial syllable, and (2) those words that can be stressed on the first or the last syllable. ... Beyond these there do not seem to be exceptions to Azerbaijani MSR cited above. It is noteworthy that MSR is one of the basic rules for the nativization of loanwords. [p.118]
world_status: statement found in an open source

The few exceptions to it, too, appear to be cl…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary word stress falls on the final syllable of the word (suffixes included); certain 'unstressable' suffixes/clitics (negative -mA-, past/copular -dI-, question mI) block it, so stress lands on the syllable immediately preceding the first such suffix. Loanwords are nativized to final stress. A small closed set of adverbs/compounds is lexically initial-stressed; vocatives and a few adverbs vary initial~final. Compounds: main stress on the second member; adjective+noun phrases: main stress on the first word.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Salimi (via SPE convention) demotes earlier-assigned final stress to secondary when an unstressable suffix pulls primary leftward (alɨ́šmadɨlàr); his review of Assaturian (p.15-16) puts secondary stress in words of >3 syllables on the root-final syllable or the first syllable. SPA 1979 (after Householder 1965 pp.xii,120) says secondary stress avoids high vowels and tends to fall on a vowel before a consonant cluster or boundary.
new_statements.exceptions: Unstressable suffixes (negative -ma-, past -di-, question mi and 'several others', cf. Damirchizada 1972:155-6); initial-stressed adverbs anjaq 'only', dünən 'yesterday', bu gün 'today', bəlkə 'perhaps'; compounds qayınana/qayınata 'mother/father-in-law'; vocatives (aná~ána 'Mother!') and adverbs burda 'here', hamısı 'all of it' vary. Mokari & Werner 2017 p.211 add imperatives (/d͡ʒǽti/ 'bring') and negatives as first-syllable-stressed cases.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress in isolation/citation forms of the author's own Tabriz speech (Salimi is a native speaker describing 'the pronunciation of the present writer', p.7 sec.1.13); phrase/compound stress treated separately (CSR/NPSR, sec. 4.2.2-4.2.3). Householder 1965 p.xiii (via SPA) likewise frames it as 'words in isolation.. louder stress and higher pitch on the last vowel'. Concordant modern statement: Mokari & Werner 2017 JIPA 47(2) p.211, 'Stress in Azerbaijani mostly falls on the final syllable of words except in some cases with imperative verbs and negative suffixes, where the stress falls on the first syllable' (file).
new_statements.identity_note: All three opened sources describe the Tabriz (Tabrizi) urban variety of Iranian Azerbaijani, the prestige norm of South Azerbaijani (Glottolog sout2697; Tabrizi is listed as a South Azerbaijani dialect). Salimi 1976 is explicitly the author's own Tabriz speech; Mokari & Werner 2017 is based on Tabriz speakers; SPA 1979/Householder 1965 is tagged 'Azerbaijani, Tabrizi' (one chief informant). Note the language name 'Azerbaijani' in these titles is undifferentiated; the North Azerbaijani standard (nort2697, Baku-based) is a different glottocode and is referenced only comparatively.

tone_statements.citation: Ahmadi, Soheila. 2024. A South Azeri variety. In Charles G. Häberl (ed.), Language Diversity in Iran: New Texts and Perspectives from Non-Iranian Languages, 5-50. Berlin/Boston: De Gruyter Mouton.
tone_statements.quote: Although stress in its general form does not cause semantic distinction, but in some cases, the meaning of the word changes by altering the position of stress, as in gæʹlin ‘come’ and gæliʹn ‘bride.’ Most Turkic languages such as Azeri have pitch accent, which is increase of the tone height on the last accentable syllable of native lexical items or word forms, such as baxʤadaʹ ‘in the garden.’ Some varieties there is a special intonation pattern at the end of yes/no-questions, possibly due to Persian influence, which replaces the interrogative particle mi.
tone_statements.locator: p. 13, sec. 3.4 'Stress and pitch accent' (whole section on p. 13) (section 757-784)
tone_statements.summary: Pitch accent: raised tone height on the last accentable syllable of native words (word stress final, some suffixes unstressable); stress place occasionally distinctive (gæʹlin 'come', gæliʹn 'bride').

Ich bezeichne diese Modulation, die natürlich nichts mit dem Wortaccent zu schaffen hat, durch — . Z. B. Türki danySysant Vergl. »Einleitung- im Anfang.

tone.translation: 7. Question intonation. Since Azeri lacks the question particle … the question is expressed by a peculiar descending modulation of the vowel of the last syllable of the last word. I mark this modulation, which of course has nothing to do with the word accent, by — . E.g. Türki danyšysan? Cf. 'Introduction' at the beginning.
